JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM): DCF Valuation Analysis

Preliminary Note on Methodology: A standard unlevered FCF DCF is not meaningful for a bank. Reported operating cash flow (-$147.8B in FY2025) is distorted by trading assets, loan originations, and deposit flows, and CapEx and FCF are not reported. I therefore use a bank-appropriate equity-cash-flow framework: projected net income, less earnings retained to support regulatory capital growth, yields distributable free cash flow to equity (FCFE) and is discounted at the cost of equity. I disclose where this departs from the requested WACC template. I use the pre-computed WACC as the stated baseline but note that cost of equity is the theoretically correct discount rate for a bank.

Revenue and Earnings Projection

Historical baseline: FY2022 $128.7B, FY2023 $158.1B, FY2024 $177.6B, FY2025 $182.4B. 3Y CAGR is 4.9% and 5Y CAGR is 2.9%, but growth is decelerating (+2.8% YoY in FY2025). Net margin has compressed from 37.0% (FY23) to 31.3% (FY25), consistent with NII normalization, deposit repricing, and higher provisions and expenses.

# RISK REPORT: JPMORGAN CHASE & CO (JPM)
**Price: $331.58 | Market Cap: ~$894B | Framework: Bridgewater principles-based risk assessment**

---

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

JPM is the best-in-class U.S. universal bank, with durable earnings, a fortress-level liquidity position, and diversified revenue. But the mechanical risk metrics the screener produces (D/E of 11.2x, negative operating cash flow) are largely artifacts of bank accounting, not distress signals. The real risks are in the **macro regime** (rising long-end yields, widening credit spreads, depressed consumer sentiment), **credit-cycle turn**, and **valuation/earnings peak risk**. Management itself is flagging private credit as a source of losses "exceeding expectations."

**Composite Risk: 4.5/10 (Moderate, below-average for a G-SIB, but with a deteriorating macro backdrop)**

---

## 1. BALANCE SHEET RISK

| Metric | Value | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Total Assets | $4.42T | Systemically important; ~15% of U.S. GDP-scale balance sheet |
| Equity | $362.4B | Equity/Assets = **8.2%** (simple leverage ~12.2x) |
| Cash | $278.8B | ~6.3% of assets; strong, though this includes central bank deposits |
| LT Debt | $267.9B | Modest relative to $4.06T liabilities; most funding is deposits |
| ROE / ROA | 15.7% / 1.3% | Excellent for the sector |

**Key observations:**

- **Debt/Equity of 11.2x is misleading.** For a bank, "debt" is mostly customer deposits, which are operating liabilities. The right lens is regulatory capital (CET1, SLR, LCR), none of which are in the provided data. This is a **data gap**: I cannot verify CET1 vs. requirement from the supplied inputs. Based on JPM's historical disclosures, it has run materially above regulatory minimums, but this should be verified against the latest 10-K/earnings release.
- **True leverage: ~12x assets/equity**, which is standard for a large universal bank and well within Basel III-type frameworks.
- **Off-balance-sheet exposure is the real blind spot:** unfunded loan commitments, derivatives notionals (tens of trillions), securities-financing and repo books, and **private credit/NBFI lending exposure**. Dimon's own warning on private credit signals that second-order exposure (bank loans to private credit funds) is a live concern.
- **Unrealized securities losses (AOCI):** With the 10Y at 4.96% (+95bp YoY) and 2Y at 4.65% (+117bp), the rate backdrop is again hostile to fixed-rate portfolio marks. JPM's hedging and HTM/AFS split mitigate this, but it is the same vulnerability that surfaced in the 2023 regional bank stress.

**Balance sheet risk score: 3/10**

# JPMORGAN CHASE & CO (JPM): Earnings Analysis

## 1. Earnings Trajectory

FY2025 net income of $57.05B (diluted EPS $20.02) declined about 2.4% from FY2024's $58.47B, even as revenue grew 2.75% to $182.45B. This is a notable inflection. FY2023 to FY2024 showed 18.0% net income growth on 12.3% revenue growth, so FY2025 marks the first period in the dataset where earnings fell while revenue rose, i.e., negative operating leverage. The 3Y and 5Y net income CAGRs (4.8% and 2.9%) now sit roughly in line with revenue CAGRs (4.9% and 2.9%), which implies earnings growth has converged to top-line growth with no incremental leverage. Net income growth of 52.4% from FY2022 ($37.68B) to FY2024 ($58.47B) is the peak-of-cycle comparison base that FY2025 is lapping.

The quarterly trend data supplied is stale (FY2013-FY2014 periods) and not usable for assessing current sequential momentum, so I make no sequential acceleration/deceleration claim from it. The more relevant recent evidence is the earnings surprise feed: four recent prints dated 2026-10-21/22 all show BEATs ($7.40 vs $6.54; $7.97 vs $7.52, among others), though the feed is unlabeled by entity/period, so I treat it as directionally supportive but low-confidence. Separately, stockanalysis.com cites TTM revenue of $190.73B (+14.1%) and net income of $64.53B (+13.7%), which, if accurate, indicates re-acceleration in 2026 versus the FY2025 annual figures. Treat this as a secondary-source datapoint, not verified against filings.

## 2. Margin Analysis

Gross and operating margins are N/A (bank income statement structure), so net margin is the usable gauge. It has compressed steadily: 36.98% (FY2023) → 32.93% (FY2024) → 31.27% (FY2025), a cumulative ~570 bps decline, with ~166 bps of that in the latest year. (The dataset contains duplicate fiscal-year labels with offset period-ends; I use period_end dates to sequence them.) Drivers cannot be confirmed from the data provided; no MD&A excerpts were supplied, so I will not attribute the compression to specific items (provisions, expense growth, net interest income normalization). The fact pattern, revenue up and net income down, points to higher expenses and/or provisions outpacing revenue. ROE of 15.7% and ROA of 1.3% remain healthy for a G-SIB.

**JPM Macro Analysis: Rate-Cushioned Earnings, Rising Credit and Valuation Risk**

**1. Macro Regime: Late-Cycle with Re-Steepening and Inflation Persistence**

The data point to a late-cycle regime, not recession or early recovery. Unemployment is 4.20% (down 0.30pp YoY), the S&P 500 is +12.1% YTD at ~$760, and VIX at 19.4 is elevated but not stressed. The warning signs are in rates and sentiment. The 10Y at 4.96% (+95bp YoY) and 2Y at 4.65% (+117bp YoY) have risen even as the Fed cut 34bp to 3.75%. That is a bear steepening in which the market is pricing sticky inflation and term premium against the Fed's easing bias. The 2s10s spread is +31bp, normalized after the inversion. CPI is up 11.2 index points YoY on a 336.3 base (~3.4%), consistent with the Fed staff estimate of 3.6% total / 3.2% core inflation. Credit spreads confirm a modest deterioration without stress: HY at 3.38% (+58bp) and IG at 0.91% (+15bp) are still tight in absolute terms but are widening from the trough.

For a $4.42T balance sheet, the key channel is the policy-rate/long-end divergence. With Fed funds at 3.75% and the 10Y at 4.96%, the curve is positively sloped by ~120bp from the front end to the 10Y. This supports net interest income through three mechanisms. # JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM): Competitive Position Analysis

**Data caveat:** The supplied SEC summary has no NIM, deposit, credit-quality, CET1, or segment data, and the external research is thin (a Ghana bankers' newsletter, a NetSuite explainer, a job posting, a Facebook post). Conclusions on moat and positioning therefore rest on the reported financials plus widely known structural features of the business. I flag where I go beyond the data. There is no peer comparison table in the context, so I cannot quantify margin premium or valuation gap against named competitors. The only peer-relative datapoint is the briefing's note that JPM's market cap is roughly 9.5x the peer median, which I cannot independently verify.

## 1. Competitive Positioning

JPM is the largest US bank by assets ($4.42T) and, on the supplied data, earns $57.05B of net income on $182.45B of revenue. A 31.3% net margin and 15.7% ROE on a ~12.2x levered balance sheet is a strong outcome for a G-SIB. ROA of 1.3% is well above the roughly 1.0% that is typically considered solid for large banks (context to verify against peers; no peer data provided).

Classification: **market leader with a diversified universal-bank model** (consumer, commercial, investment banking, markets, asset and wealth management). Differentiation comes from breadth and scale rather than from a single product. A franchise like this can cross-sell, fund itself cheaply, and absorb credit and market cycles better than monoline competitors.

**Pricing power is hard to read from this data, and the margin trend is a yellow flag.** Net margin has compressed from 36.1% (FY23) to 32.9% to 32.1% to 31.3%, about 480 bps, while revenue grew. Revenue growth also slowed to 2.8% YoY versus a 4.9% 3-year CAGR. The data cannot say whether the cause is deposit repricing, higher provisions, expense growth, or normalization from an unusually favorable FY23 rate environment. The most defensible reading is normalization from a cyclical peak, not erosion of franchise quality, but that is an inference, not something the data confirms. Note also that the revenue series carries what looks like a one-off step-up in FY23 (from $128.7B to $158.1B, +22.8%), so the 3-year CAGR flatters the underlying run-rate. The 5-year CAGR of 2.9% is the cleaner read of structural growth.

Two data hygiene points: operating cash flow of -$147.78B is not meaningful for a bank. Cash flow statements for banks are dominated by trading assets, loans originated, and deposit flows, so I place no analytical weight on it, and "free cash flow" does not apply. Likewise, the reported debt/equity of 11.2x is mostly deposits and other liabilities, not funded leverage in the industrial sense.
